2. Who donated seeds?
3. Who received part of the harvest?
4. What larger benefit did the garden create?
readings.answers:
1. Little money and almost no equipment.
2. Several families.
3. Older residents who had difficulty reaching the market.
4. A space for cooperation and learning.
readings.languageFocus: Vocabulary: donate, harvest, volunteer, portion, organiser. Grammar: contrast, relative clauses, modals.

readings.title: Learning in a Digital World
readings.passage: Online courses have made education more accessible for many learners. A person who lives far from a university can now attend lectures without travelling. Digital platforms also allow students to pause a lesson, review difficult points, and practise at their own pace. These advantages are important, but access to technology is not equal. Some learners lack reliable internet connections, and others share one device with their entire family. Moreover, not every online course offers meaningful feedback or opportunities for discussion. Effective learning requires more than watching videos. Learners benefit when they set goals, test their understanding, and receive useful feedback. Teachers can support them by providing clear instructions and varied activities. Online education may therefore expand opportunities, but its success depends on thoughtful design and access to resources. A balanced policy should consider both the potential benefits and the practical barriers.
readings.grammarNotes: “have made” သည် present perfect (လက်ရှိအကျိုးသက်ရောက်မှု), “may expand” သည် cautious prediction, “who lives ...” သည် defining relative clause ဖြစ်သည်။
readings.questions:
1. Give two benefits of online learning.
2. Name two barriers.
3. Why may watching videos be insufficient?
4. Is the author completely positive about online learning? Explain.
readings.answers:
1. Distance access and flexible review/pacing.
2. Unreliable internet and limited device access.
3. Goals, practice and feedback are also needed.
4. No; the author balances benefits with barriers.
readings.languageFocus: Vocabulary: accessible, reliable, meaningful, opportunity, barrier. Grammar: present perfect, relative clause, hedging.

readings.title: What Can a Survey Tell Us?
readings.passage: A survey can reveal useful patterns in public opinion, but its findings must be interpreted carefully. Imagine that a researcher asks one hundred people in a shopping centre whether they support a new transport policy. Sixty respondents say yes. It might be tempting to announce that 60 per cent of all residents support the policy. That conclusion would be too strong. People who visit the shopping centre may differ from those who do not, and the sample may not reflect the wider population. The wording of the question can also influence responses. For example, a question that describes the policy as “a necessary solution to traffic problems” may produce different answers from a neutral question. To evaluate a survey, readers should examine how participants were selected, how questions were phrased, and whether the reported uncertainty is reasonable. Surveys can inform decisions, but they do not remove the need for judgement.
readings.grammarNotes: “can reveal / may differ / might be tempting” တို့သည် certainty အဆင့်ကွာသော modal expressions ဖြစ်သည်။ ဤစာပိုဒ်၏ အဓိကသင်ခန်းစာမှာ sample representativeness နှင့် question wording ဖြစ်သည်။
readings.questions:
1. What percentage supported the policy in the sample?
2. Why can that percentage not simply describe all residents?
3. How can wording affect survey responses?
4. Name two checks a critical reader should make.
readings.answers:
1. 60%.
2. The sample may not represent the whole population.
3. Leading wording can change answers.
4. Sampling, question wording and uncertainty (any two).
readings.languageFocus: Vocabulary: respondent, sample, population, neutral, judgement. Grammar: modality, relative clauses, conditional reasoning.

readings.title: Why Clear Language Matters in Public Policy
readings.passage: A public policy may be technically sound yet fail to achieve its aims if the people affected cannot understand it. Consider a notice that tells residents to “initiate the submission of documentary evidence prior to the termination of the application period”. The message may be grammatically correct, but its meaning is unnecessarily difficult to process. A clearer version would be: “Send your supporting documents before the application deadline.” The second sentence identifies the action, the object and the deadline without changing the basic instruction. Plain language is not the same as oversimplification. Complex policies sometimes require precise legal or technical terms, and replacing those terms carelessly may produce ambiguity. The challenge is to explain specialist concepts accurately while removing avoidable obstacles. Good public communication therefore demands both linguistic precision and an understanding of the audience. It also requires feedback: a message that appears clear to its author may confuse people who encounter it for the first time. Testing a notice with actual users can reveal difficulties that a policy team did not anticipate.
readings.grammarNotes: “may ... yet ...” က unexpected contrast ဖြစ်သည်။ Nominalisation နှင့် plain-language version ကို နှိုင်းထားပြီး “a message that appears clear ...” သည် relative clause ဖြစ်သည်။
readings.questions:
1. What is wrong with the original notice?
2. What does the revised sentence improve?
3. Why should technical terms not always be removed?
4. What can user testing reveal?
readings.answers:
1. It is unnecessarily complex.
2. It makes the action, object and deadline clear.
3. They can be necessary for accuracy.
4. Unexpected comprehension barriers.
readings.languageFocus: Vocabulary: ambiguity, initiate, submission, obstacle, precision. Grammar: concessive contrast, nominalisation, relative clauses.

readings.title: The Risk of Overconfident Conclusions
readings.passage: A striking headline can make a scientific finding seem more certain than it is. Suppose a small observational study reports an association between a particular habit and improved concentration. A news article might translate that result into the claim that the habit “makes people smarter”. This transformation changes the scope of the original evidence. The study may not have measured intelligence, and its design may not allow researchers to establish causation. Even where an association is genuine, other variables could explain some or all of the observed pattern. None of this means that observational research is worthless. Such studies can identify questions worth investigating and can provide evidence when experiments are impractical or unethical. The appropriate response is neither unquestioning acceptance nor automatic dismissal. Instead, readers should ask what was measured, how participants were selected, what alternative explanations were considered and whether independent studies have produced comparable results. The quality of a conclusion depends not only on the data collected but also on the care with which the inference is drawn.
readings.grammarNotes: ဤစာပိုဒ်တွင် epistemic caution: may, could, cannot establish, comparable results တို့ ပါဝင်သည်။ “neither ... nor ...” သည် အလွန်အမင်းသဘောထားနှစ်ဘက်လုံးကို ငြင်းပြီး balanced stance ဖော်ပြသည်။
readings.questions:
1. What is the difference between the study and the headline?
2. Why might other variables matter?
3. Does the passage reject observational research?
4. What is a balanced response to such claims?
readings.answers:
1. The study reports an association; the headline asserts a causal improvement in intelligence.
2. They could explain the apparent relationship.
3. No. It says such studies can be useful.
4. Examine methods, measurements, alternatives and replication.
readings.languageFocus: Vocabulary: observational, association, causation, inference, comparable. Grammar: cautious claims, contrast, dense noun phrases.

readings.title: Two Visions of a Better City
readings.passage: When a city debates its future, disagreements are rarely confined to buildings and roads. Beneath technical arguments about housing density, public transport and zoning lie competing ideas about whose needs should take priority. One proposal may promise economic growth by attracting investment, while another may insist that affordability and social inclusion deserve greater attention. Neither position can be assessed adequately through slogans alone. It is necessary to ask who is expected to benefit, who might bear the costs and which assumptions support the predicted outcomes. A transport project, for example, may reduce average travel time while making access more difficult for certain neighbourhoods. An apparently efficient solution can therefore produce uneven consequences. Good evaluation requires both quantitative indicators and informed accounts of lived experience. Yet the choice of indicators is itself consequential: what a government measures tends to shape what it notices. A more transparent debate would acknowledge these trade-offs openly, examine uncertainty and invite affected residents into decision-making. Such participation cannot guarantee consensus, but it can make the reasoning behind public choices more visible and more accountable.
readings.grammarNotes: “Beneath ... lie competing ideas” သည် locative inversion ဖြစ်ပြီး C2 ပုံစံတစ်ခုဖြစ်သည်။ “Neither ... alone” နှင့် “while” က balanced comparison ပေးသည်။ ဘာသာစကားနဲ့ ရှုပ်ထွေးသော policy argument တည်ဆောက်ပုံကို လေ့လာပါ။
readings.questions:
1. What lies beneath apparently technical disagreements?
2. Why are average outcomes potentially misleading?
3. What limitation of indicators does the passage identify?
4. What can participation improve, even without consensus?
readings.answers:
1. Conflicting priorities and views of whose needs matter.
2. They can conceal unequal effects on different groups.
3. Indicator choice shapes what decision-makers notice.
4. Transparency and accountability of reasoning.
readings.languageFocus: Vocabulary: density, zoning, affordability, trade-off, accountability. Grammar: inversion, concession, nuanced contrast.

writings.title: A Personal Introduction

writings.modelAnswer: My name is May. I live in a small city with my family. I study English every evening because I want to communicate with people from different countries. I enjoy reading stories and learning new words. My favourite subject is history. On weekends, I often visit the library with my sister. I hope to become a confident English speaker.

writings.title: Describing a Past Experience
writings.task: ခရီးတစ်ခု သို့မဟုတ် နေ့ထူးနေ့မြတ်ကို စာလုံး ၁၀၀–၁၃၀ ရေးပါ။ Past simple နှင့် past continuous ကိုတွဲသုံးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer: Last year, I visited a historic town with two friends. We arrived early in the morning and walked through the market. While we were taking photographs, an elderly shopkeeper invited us to try a local snack. She explained how it was made and told us a story about the town. We thanked her and continued our walk. Before we left, we bought a few books about local history. The trip was memorable because we learned more than we had expected.
writings.whyItWorks: We arrived / walked က sequence၊ were taking က background၊ had expected က past-before-past ဖြစ်သည်။

writings.title: An Informal Email
writings.task: မိတ်ဆွေကို သင်တန်းအကြောင်း ပြောပြီး အကြံတောင်းသော informal email စာလုံး ၁၀၀–၁၄၀ ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer:
Subject: My new English course
Hi Aye,
I have recently joined an online English course, and I am enjoying it. The lessons are short, but the exercises are challenging. I have been practising for half an hour every day. I still find articles and prepositions difficult, so I am keeping a notebook of useful examples.
Have you tried any good vocabulary-learning methods? I would love to hear your suggestions. Maybe we could practise speaking together next weekend.
Best wishes,
May

writings.title: A Formal Request Email
writings.task: သင်တန်းအချက်အလက် တောင်းဆိုသည့် formal email ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer:
Subject: Request for Course Information
Dear Admissions Team,
I am writing to request further information about your advanced English programme. Could you please confirm the entry requirements, course schedule and total fees? I would also appreciate details of any scholarships or fee reductions that may be available.
If possible, please let me know whether the course includes academic writing and reading practice.
Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours faithfully,
May

writings.title: An Opinion Paragraph
writings.task: “Online learning can expand access to education” ဆိုသည့်အဆိုကို စာလုံး ၁၂၀–၁၆၀ ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer: Online learning can expand access to education, particularly for people who live far from training centres. Because lessons can be recorded, learners are often able to study at convenient times and review difficult material. This flexibility may benefit people who work or provide care at home. However, online courses do not automatically guarantee equal opportunities. Reliable internet, suitable devices and meaningful feedback are still necessary. Schools and policymakers should therefore combine digital provision with practical support for learners who face barriers. In this way, technology can become a tool for inclusion rather than another source of inequality.
writings.whyItWorks: Topic sentence → explanation → limitation → recommendation → concluding implication ဖြစ်သည်။ may benefit သည် hedging၊ However သည် contrast ဖြစ်သည်။
writings.checklist: topic sentence; reason; example; counterpoint; clear final sentence

writings.title: A Problem–Solution Essay
writings.task: “Reducing misinformation” ကို စာလုံး ၂၀၀ ခန့်၊ အဖွင့်–အဓိကပိုဒ်–နိဂုံး ဖြင့်ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer:
Misinformation can spread quickly when information is shared without careful checking. Although digital platforms allow people to communicate efficiently, they can also amplify inaccurate claims. A useful response must address both individual habits and institutional responsibilities.
First, people need practical media-literacy skills. Before sharing a dramatic headline, readers should check the publication date, identify the original source and compare the claim with reliable reporting. Schools can teach these skills through realistic examples rather than abstract warnings.
Second, institutions should communicate clearly and correct errors transparently. When official information is difficult to understand or slow to appear, rumours may fill the gap. Timely explanations, accessible language and visible corrections can help build trust.
No single measure will eliminate misinformation. Nevertheless, stronger checking habits and more accountable communication can reduce its influence without discouraging open discussion.
writings.whyItWorks: Problem definition → two solutions → proportionate conclusion. “can/may” အသုံးက absolute claim ရှောင်ထားသည်။
writings.checklist: clear thesis; parallel solution paragraphs; cautious claims; cohesive conclusion

writings.title: A Balanced Argument Essay
writings.task: “Should public transport be free?” ဆိုသည့် မေးခွန်းအတွက် balance ပါသော စာလုံး ၂၂၀ ခန့်ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer:
Free public transport is often proposed as a way to reduce inequality and traffic congestion. Supporters argue that removing fares can make essential services more accessible to people with low incomes. If reliable transport becomes easier to use, some residents may also choose buses or trains instead of private cars.
However, fare-free systems still require substantial funding. The absence of ticket revenue may increase pressure on public budgets, particularly where existing services are already unreliable. Moreover, lower fares alone may not change travel behaviour if routes are infrequent or inaccessible.
A sensible approach would examine local conditions rather than assuming that one policy will succeed everywhere. In some cities, targeted discounts and improved services might produce greater benefits than universal fare removal. In others, a well-funded fare-free programme could be effective.
The most defensible choice is therefore the one supported by evidence about cost, accessibility, ridership and distributional effects. The aim should not be free transport as a slogan, but transport that is fair, practical and sustainable.
writings.whyItWorks: Supporting view, counterargument, qualified conclusion; might/could က context-dependent policy effect ကို ဖော်ပြသည်။
writings.checklist: clear comparison; fair opposing view; evidence needs; nuanced conclusion

writings.title: A Research Summary
writings.task: ပေးထားသော ရလဒ်ကို original meaning မပျောက်စေဘဲ cautious academic summary ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer:
This hypothetical study examines whether short daily reading sessions are associated with vocabulary growth among adult learners. Participants completed a vocabulary test before and after
a six-week programme. The group that reported more consistent reading showed greater average improvement. However, the study was observational, and the sample was relatively small. The findings therefore suggest an association rather than demonstrating that reading time alone caused the improvement. Further research with larger and more representative samples would be needed before broader conclusions could be drawn.
writings.whyItWorks: This hypothetical study ဟု example ဖြစ်ကြောင်းဖော်ပြသည်။ associated with, suggest, rather than demonstrating, would be needed သည် scientific caution ဖြစ်သည်။
writings.checklist: purpose; method; finding; limitation; implication; accurate hedging

writings.title: A Policy Brief Executive Summary
writings.task: ပြည်သူ့ဝန်ဆောင်မှု သတင်းအချက်အလက် ပိုမိုလက်လှမ်းမီရေး အကြံပြုချက်ကို ၁၈၀ စကားလုံးဝန်းကျင် ရေးပါ။
writings.modelAnswer:
Executive Summary
Complex forms and unclear instructions can prevent residents from accessing services to which they are entitled. This brief recommends a plain-language review of frequently used public forms, supported by testing with diverse users.
The proposed approach has three elements. First, agencies should identify the steps that applicants most often misunderstand. Second, revised forms should use direct instructions, consistent terminology and examples where necessary. Third, testing should include people with different levels of literacy and digital access.
Success should be assessed through measurable outcomes, including application-completion rates, correction requests and user feedback. The reform would require staff time and coordination, but its potential benefits include fewer avoidable errors and more equitable access.
A phased pilot is recommended before wider implementation. This would allow agencies to identify unintended difficulties, adjust the design and make decisions using evidence rather than assumptions.
